step_marks.step_description: Definition of mutable vs immutable types in Python
Valid code example showing list mutability vs tuple/string immutability

Q1.model_answer: In Python, mutable data types allow modification of their state or contents in-place without changing object identity (e.g. list, dict, set). Immutable types cannot be modified once created (e.g. int, float, str, tuple). Modifying an immutable type creates a new object in memory.

step_marks.step_description: Explanation of LEGB rule (Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in)
Role and syntax of the 'global' keyword in modifying module-level variables

Q2.model_answer: Python resolves variable scope using the LEGB rule: Local (inside current function), Enclosing (in outer enclosing defs), Global (module namespace), and Built-in (built-in keywords and exceptions). To modify a global variable inside a local scope, the 'global' keyword must be explicitly declared before assignment.

step_marks.step_description: Correct definition of Stack and LIFO principle
Implementation of Push function with overflow check or append
Implementation of Pop function with underflow check and return

Q3.model_answer: A stack is a linear data structure that adheres to the Last In First Out (LIFO) principle. Operations: Push: def push(stack, item): stack.append(item). Pop: def pop(stack): if len(stack) == 0: return 'Underflow' else: return stack.pop().

step_marks.step_description: SQL query with GROUP BY clause on Department
Correct usage of HAVING clause to filter aggregate COUNT(*) > 5 or AVG(Salary) > 50000

Q4.model_answer: SELECT Department, COUNT(*), AVG(Salary) FROM Employee GROUP BY Department HAVING COUNT(*) > 5; The GROUP BY clause groups rows sharing attribute values, while HAVING filters groups based on aggregate conditions (unlike WHERE which filters individual rows).
